title: A less stable molecule outnumbers its sturdier twin in interstellar space
freshness: Astronomy & Astrophysics-accepted paper posted to arXiv on October 29, 2026; selected within the preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: Radio observations have identified HNCOH+ in space for the first time inside a chemically rich cloud near the Galactic Center. The ion is almost four times as abundant as a more stable arrangement of the same atoms, showing that interstellar chemistry is governed by reaction pathways as well as molecular stability.
whyItMatters: Chemical models often begin by asking which molecular arrangement has the lowest energy. This detection shows why formation rates and barriers also matter, helping astronomers reconstruct how carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen combine before stars and planets form.
whatToExploreNext: Why can a faster reaction pathway make a less stable isomer more abundant than its lower-energy counterpart?

sources.label: Rey-Montejo et al., Detection of HNCOH+ in the interstellar medium

body:
## A new ion in a cloud near the Galactic Center

Astronomers have identified HNCOH+ in interstellar space for the first time. The ion was found in G+0.693-0.027, a molecular cloud near the center of the Milky Way whose shocks release a rich mixture of molecules from dust grains into surrounding gas.

HNCOH+ contains hydrogen, nitrogen, carbon, and oxygen. It is a protonated form of isocyanic acid, meaning that the neutral molecule has gained a proton. Its atoms can be connected in more than one arrangement. Such arrangements are called isomers: they contain the same numbers of each atom but differ in structure, much as the same set of building pieces can form different shapes.

The newly detected arrangement attaches the extra proton through oxygen. Another isomer, H2NCO+, places it through nitrogen and has lower energy, making it more stable under equilibrium conditions. The surprise is that the less stable HNCOH+ is much more abundant in this cloud.

## Listening for a molecular fingerprint

Molecules rotate at specific energy levels. When they change rotational state, they emit or absorb radio waves at characteristic frequencies. A collection of these spectral lines acts like a molecular fingerprint.

The team searched an ultra-deep survey covering nearly 150 gigahertz of bandwidth between 31 and 275 gigahertz. The observations came from the Yebes 40-meter telescope in Spain, the IRAM 30-meter telescope in Spain, and the APEX telescope in Chile. The survey included eight predicted HNCOH+ transitions. Four fell into gaps in frequency coverage, and one more was excluded because it blended with an atmospheric feature. The remaining pattern included three nearly unblended lines and a broader sequence that matched one velocity and excitation temperature.

That consistency supports the identification, but there is a technical limit. Laboratory experiments had measured only the two lowest rotational transitions directly. Frequencies at shorter millimeter wavelengths were extrapolated from those data. Their uncertainties are small compared with the broad lines in this cloud, and the fitted distortion parameter agrees with quantum-chemical calculations. Even so, the authors say dedicated laboratory spectroscopy is needed for a fuller rotational map.

The fitted column density is 9.9 plus or minus 0.5 trillion molecules per square centimeter along the telescope's sightline. Relative to molecular hydrogen, the abundance is about 7 parts in 100 billion. HNCOH+ is 3.8 times as abundant as H2NCO+, with an uncertainty of roughly half a unit in that ratio.

## Reaction routes can beat the lowest-energy outcome

If the two isomers settled into thermodynamic equilibrium, the lower-energy H2NCO+ form should dominate overwhelmingly. Instead, kinetic calculations offer a different explanation. When HNCO reacts with H3+, the pathway that produces HNCOH+ is predicted to receive about 80 percent of the products, compared with about 20 percent for H2NCO+. A high barrier then makes conversion from one form to the other unlikely. The molecules preserve the history of how they formed rather than simply rearranging into the most stable option.

The isocyanate group in HNCOH+ is also part of the backbone structure found in peptide bonds. That chemical connection makes the ion relevant to studies of prebiotic chemistry, but it must not be overstated. HNCOH+ is not a peptide or a protein, and its detection is not evidence of life. It shows that one small piece of biologically useful chemistry can arise in a cold interstellar environment.

**Measured:** a consistent set of rotational lines, the ion's column density, and an abundance almost four times that of its more stable isomer in one Galactic Center cloud.

**Inferred:** fast formation of HNCOH+ and a large conversion barrier probably explain why the less stable structure persists.
